original:
Borrow One Competency at a Time
A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age, but it’s not just a foolish waste of time. It’s actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great guide. Maybe an older sibling protected you well. And there’s always your future healed self if you can imagine that.
For warmth, think of someone you remember fondly. How would they sit beside your little one? Just make sure it’s someone who liked you the way you were.
For protecting, ask what a minimally competent adult would do here. Maybe something simple, like actually smelling that old food you’re about to eat and then trashing it if it smells a little weird. If you’re about to send an angry text, hit pause. If the room itself triggers your spidey sense, leave, or lock the door and get help. Even if this still feels like the child acting like the adult, for now, that’s ok. “Fake it til you make it” isn’t exactly it, but yeah. Afterward, you can tell your little one, “I did that for us. That was the Protector.” If it sounds funny, laugh!
The Guide can be you too, just a calmer you. That’s a lot easier to imagine than your future healed self. Think back to what (and how) you decided about something like this the last time you were calm. Or ask what the wise person you respect would have you practice today. A wise tradition (like “What would Jesus do?” or “What would Buddha do?”) can give some direction, too, until you develop your own internal compass.

original: Where it really differs is spirituality. original: The closest thing I can compare it to is the out-of-body part of some near-death experiences. People sometimes report seeing things from impossible angles, and some of those reports (controversially) were verified by others in the room. My room event had nothing like that to check, though, since I wasn’t floating around noticing any details. So those cases can’t back mine up. They just help me show what I mean by an experience that wasn’t stuck at the body’s vantage point anymore. If you want to go down that rabbit hole, there’s this systematic analysis of near-death reports, the AWARE-II cardiac-arrest study, and a recent veridical-NDE evidence scale.

original: Sometimes you have a really good session where you feel how much you care about your little one and say what they needed to hear. A few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. For a lot of people, the first thought is that they didn’t go deep enough. I doubt that’s the problem, and the session doesn’t sound like a failure to me. Try a tiny bit of what you did for your little one as you go about your day, because one small thing like that can teach them more than ten more good meditations. Text a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine, for instance. Sending that text can be harder than the meditation was.

original: In SN 22.22 the Buddha puts the weight in one place and the carrying in another. The five aggregates are the burden, and craving is what picks it up. The tangle is heavy all by itself (even an arahant still feels the first dart), and craving is why we keep lugging it around. Physics backs this up, and I mean literally: quarks supply less than 1% of a proton’s mass, and roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy. Matter weighs what its binding weighs. Light weighs nothing.

Light, on the other hand, weighs nothing.

original: I used to attribute “life is like a dream” directly to the historical Buddha. The famous stanza I loved is actually from the later Mahāyāna Diamond Sutra, which puts some words in his mouth. The early Pāli texts were already reaching for the same kind of pictures, though. In SN 22.95 form is like foam, feeling is like a bubble, perception is a mirage and consciousness is a magic trick, and Dhammapada 170 tells us to look at the world like a bubble, or a mirage.

original:
Forgiveness without bypass
We cannot force forgiveness on ourselves. It has to come from a place of understanding, otherwise it can be bypassing. However, if we remain in the anger forever, we are allowing the injury to dictate how we live our lives in the present. So how do we hold all of this? We just remember that it can all be true at once. They really did hurt us and they still have to answer for it. Our boundary with them is crucial to maintain, especially after forgiveness which can tend to weaken it. One day we may find that we have forgiven them for not knowing better, just like Jesus did on the Cross.
You might say to the part of you that got hurt, “I’m not going to use spiritual mumbo jumbo to shush your cries and make you forgive before you're ready. But I’m also not going to build our whole life around this wound forever.”
Forgiving yourself
For self-forgiveness, name what you regret doing, and take responsibility for just that part. Let yourself feel the remorse by taking in the harm done. See how it went against your values. Stop short of making yourself a permanent criminal by identifying with the behaviors you're now abandoning.
Do what you can to put it right. Every so often, come back to how you got to be someone who could do that, until you understand the pattern well enough that it can't drive you anymore.

original: Milder reactions afterward count as caution signs too, like getting confused or spaced out (dissociating) again and again. Get professional help right away if any of this is severe or risky, and especially if it keeps going or comes back while you’re sober. Don’t suddenly quit a prescribed medicine, or anything your body is dependent on, just because it might be part of the problem; have a doctor help you stop safely.
rewrite: Say you keep feeling confused or spaced out afterward. That’s one of the milder reactions, but those count as caution signs too. And if a prescribed medicine, or anything your body is dependent on, might be part of the problem, don’t suddenly quit it; have a doctor help you stop safely.

original: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. Maybe you’ve left a family or community, maybe you’ve stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you’re doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing. For a while the old you is gone and the new you hasn’t shown up yet. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state like that a bardo.

A therapist or helper might step back because you’re doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing.

original: Differentiation is slow, and it goes on your whole life. If a family, group or relationship won’t let you do this while you’re still part of it, temporary distance may be necessary. And sometimes you need the break anyway, because it’s hard to hear what you actually want while the old programming is still playing in your ear. Some people come back later on different terms. Sometimes the leaving turns out to be permanent, because going back would mean disappearing again. You don’t have to know yet which one yours is. As you differentiate, you learn to tell the difference.

original:
I think the opposite trap can feel a lot like finally having your act together. It’s forced adulthood, and it sounds like “Nope, all good!” from somebody with a fever who’s cleaning the whole kitchen anyway. Not a lot of fun in that kitchen, and nobody gets very close to the person in it. If that’s you, clamping down harder is going to feel like the fix, but it’s just more of the same. I’d try croaking to someone you trust, “Could you pick up some soup?” If you keep swinging between spoiling and clamping down, try staying warm while you say what happens next, like “Not now, we’ll go after lunch.”
Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it’s okay to want a lot of closeness. So then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you’ve texted “hello??” before they’re at the corner. When they get back, you sulk all night. Wanting them close is fine! Blowing up their phone and sulking all night is a different story. Your Guide could help you ask for what you need instead, like a hug before they go and a rough idea of when they’ll be back. Before any of that, though, I’d let your little one say what’s going on. I think it just wants to know they’re coming back.
The Guide doesn’t need to know everything for sure (that would be an OCD Guide, and then you’d need a Guide for the OCD Guide). It chooses the next sane step that fits your values based on the info available, and that’s how it helps your little one grow toward a whole life. Waiting to be sure first is sometimes proper & prudent, but if it’s a pattern, it can keep life on hold, and then your little one’s world stays small. Sometimes something really is stuck on someone else’s end (you’ve asked, and followed up, and there’s nothing left for you to do yet), and waiting on that isn’t avoidance. The Guide can let it wait, keeping an eye out for when it frees up, and keep the rest of your life moving, so your little one keeps growing anyway.

original: One important thing to become aware of when approaching your inner child is your inherited parent script. Your parent script is made up of a collection of rules and ways of treating yourself that you adopted as a child (mostly based on how you were treated by your parent(s)). It doesn’t always take the form of a voice. It is not the inner adult (Nurturer, Protector, Guide) that you consciously build. Often this script acts as a critic or warden, telling your inner child not to cry, not to be “needy”, not to embarrass them, not to be too independent, etc. So when you begin talking to your child in a new, loving way, the script may jump in to say that what you’re doing is “fake”.
rewrite: When you’re approaching your inner child, it’s important to be aware of the parent script you inherited. It’s made up of the rules and ways of treating yourself that you picked up as a child, mostly from how your parent(s) treated you. It doesn’t always come as a voice, and it isn’t the inner adult (Nurturer, Protector, Guide) that you consciously build. Often this script acts as a critic or warden, telling your inner child not to cry, not to be “needy”, not to embarrass them, not to be too independent, etc. So when you begin talking to your child in a new, loving way, the script may jump in to say that what you’re doing is “fake”.

original: That part doesn’t have to move out. It’s been living there way longer than the grown-up you. It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one. I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there’s a grown-up here now who could call it all off if things got to be too much. It doesn’t have to be all or nothing, either. Maybe it would settle for a lighter cover for now, like blinds tilted open a crack, and let you peek out for a minute (ST-CA, section 9.3.4). If it says no, I’d listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all.

original:
Borrow Hindsight
I sometimes ask: “How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?” It’s a question borrowed from your future self, and I wouldn’t take their answer as gospel. I don’t think a perfect Higher Self is waiting in there with the answers, either (more on that in How This Relates to IFS).
That future you also knows why you can’t pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here? Maybe they’d just make you some food. If you can’t picture them, make the food yourself, and don’t bother faking a feeling first. A “no” or a pause can count as the food, too.
You can borrow a wiser future version of whoever else is involved, too, as long as you don’t assume they’ll end up on your side, or sorry. What the current one keeps doing is still what you go by, however good the picture looks (the future one has never called you back).

original: This power to remove people is so easily abused, though. So work out the process before it’s about anyone in particular. What counts as cause for immediate protective action? Who has to step aside because they’re too close to it? Who decides to put temporary restrictions on someone? Who will make sure all the evidence is preserved? How will the person be able to reply to the concerns? What review or appeal is possible without endangering others? What protections will there be for the person’s interests (housing, records, family contact, access to common resources, outside funds if any) during the separation? When is it time to bring in outside help?

Being worn out can stop you too, and sometimes whoever said they’d help couldn’t make it. Hey, we’ve all been there. 🤗

Plenty of seekers and gurus do it too; I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example. I did it too. It doesn’t mean you’re stupid or crazy.
